analysis: Docs-only PR; no executable code or config changed in the supplied units. docs/provider/cli-reference.md: the only changed line visible in the supplied text is head line 1716, a new passthrough-table row for DARKBLOOM_GLM_PERSISTENT_WIRED_RESIDENCY. The row says it is on by default and that 0/false/no/off rolls back to per-command-buffer residency. This is a performance/memory knob and touches no auth, attestation, encryption, billing or key-handling surface. The other changed range, head lines 17-60 (Local GLM qualification), is only in the patch excerpt, which is truncated, so it was not reviewed in detail. From the visible excerpt it describes an opt-in via an absolute qualification JSON through DARKBLOOM_EXPERIMENTAL_GLM5_NEXT, which is not forwarded to launchd and does not bypass memory admission. That is consistent with the TB-003/TB-007 posture, but the statement that the encrypted checkpoint identity records the GLM execution policy was cut off and could not be verified. The rest of the unit text (lines 835-1783, cache env vars, T-041 prefix-cache defaults, App Attest worker opt-in) is unchanged context that is consistent with the existing threat model. docs/provider/direct-mode.md: only metadata and a truncated patch were supplied, with no numbered text. The patch shows that the /v1/responses description changed from 'in-memory store' to 'provider continuation history and SDK response-object storage, with distinct retention below', and that a new section 'Responses continuation and retention' (head 157-182) was added. This could mean prompt or response content is retained locally for longer or in a different place. That would matter for A-001 and TB-003 (operator access to plaintext) but is local direct-mode scope. Its content could not be seen, so I made no determination. The next pass should read the full retention section, check that the stated retention/storage matches the implementation, and check that any on-disk persistence is encrypted or access-controlled. It should also check that the docs do not understate consumer-prompt exposure on the provider. No findings.
